title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: In defence electronics, you do not have a salesforce knocking on doors; you have an engineering team spending five years inside a DRDO lab so that your part number is written into the system specification.
epigraph.author: Defence Procurement Reality

web_blocks.html: Astra Microwave has no retail network, no dealers, and zero consumer ad spend. Its sales channel is direct B2G and B2B defence OEM qualification [4, 12]. Every rupee of domestic revenue flows through a strict institutional funnel. Buyers include DRDO labs (LRDE for radars, DLRL for EW, DRDL for missiles), defence PSUs (BEL and HAL), ISRO centres (SAC and URSC), and the IMD [6, 12, 17]. Once Astra qualifies as a Development-cum-Production Partner (DcPP), switching suppliers mid-programme is costly [7, 9, 17]. A buyer would have to repeat years of environmental, EMI/EMC, and flight-clearance tests, creating high switching barriers [7, 9, 17].

In exports, Astra skips end-government sales and plugs into global Tier-1 supply chains [12, 13]. It serves Israeli and European primes like Rafael, Elbit, and Thales, often driven by Indian MoD offset rules [12, 13]. That split creates two very different margin profiles. Export build-to-print orders use customer-supplied or imported MMIC kits and earn 12%–16% operating margins [12, 13]. By contrast, domestic IP-led production—where Astra owns the RF design and localises assembly—earns 28%–33% operating margins [12, 13, 14].

Semiconductor and RF part lead times are the main supply chain bottleneck [4]. High-power GaN and GaAs MMIC dies, space-grade FPGAs, precision connectors, and RF laminates come mostly from US, European, and Taiwanese foundries. Defence contracts impose stiff fines for late delivery. To avoid delays, Astra buys long-lead imported chips 6 to 12 months before customer delivery dates [1, 4]. That buffer explains why inventory days stretched to 389 days in FY25 and 394 days in FY26 [1, 4].

Manufacturing and testing sit across two southern Indian aerospace hubs [6, 7]. In Hyderabad (Telangana), Astra runs five units across Bollaram (Units 1 & 2) and Maheshwaram Hardware Park / E-City (Units 3, 4 & 7) [6, 7]. These sites house Class 10,000 and Class 100,000 cleanrooms, SMT lines, chip-and-wire bonding, 3D X-ray checks, and stress chambers [6, 7]. In Bengaluru (Karnataka), Astra runs an R&D and integration hub at the Aerospace Park near the airport, right next to HAL and LRDE [6]. Astra also owns Near Field and Far Field Antenna Test Ranges (NFTR/FFTR) and an NABL-accredited EMI/EMC chamber up to 40 GHz [8, 9]. Having those labs in-house removes external test queues that slow down smaller peers [8, 9].

web_blocks.caption: FY26 Consolidated Unit Economics Waterfall (₹1,163 Cr Revenue → ₹193 Cr PAT → ₹304 Cr FCF)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every ₹100 of FY26 revenue, ₹50.5 went to materials/inventory, ₹13.3 to specialised engineering talent, and ₹7.5 to other opex, leaving ₹28.7 in EBITDA and ₹16.6 in net profit—while working-capital release lifted CFO to ₹33.3 per ₹100 of sales [1, 2].

web_blocks.html: Billing and cash conversion are the hardest parts of Astra's unit economics [4]. Domestic B2G buyers (BEL, HAL, DRDO, IMD) inspect hardware in batches and pay only after milestone sign-offs. As a result, sales and cash collections bunch heavily in Q4. March-quarter sales hit ₹488 Cr in FY26—42% of full-year revenue—versus just ₹177 Cr in Q1 FY27 [1]. With 394 inventory days and 216 debtor days (down from 273 in FY25), Astra's Cash Conversion Cycle reached 537 days in FY26 [1]. That heavy working-capital load forces Astra to pay ₹56 Cr in annual finance costs (4.8% of sales) despite earning 28.7% EBITDA margins [1].

A typical domestic AESA radar or EW contract shows why gross margins stay high while cash stays tied up [4, 12]. Contracts are fixed-price or capped-escalation, won after competitive or single-vendor DcPP qualification [12, 17]. Raw materials—chiefly imported GaN/GaAs MMICs, RF circuit boards, metal housings, and connectors—take roughly 50.5% of sales (₹587.3 Cr net of stock changes in FY26) [1, 2]. After cleanroom assembly in Hyderabad, every unit goes through RF calibration, thermal cycling (-40°C to +85°C), vibration checks, and NFTR verification [7, 8, 9]. Customer teams (DGAQA, BEL, or HAL) must then sign off before dispatch [7, 8, 9]. Only after delivery and acceptance testing can Astra issue the final milestone bill [4].

Government defence budgets expire every March 31, so public-sector buyers cluster inspections and fund releases into January–March [1, 4]. That calendar forces Astra to hold peak raw materials and work-in-progress through Q1–Q3. Borrowings rose to ₹487 Cr by September 2026 before converting into Q4 sales (₹488 Cr in Q4 FY26) and cash [1, 14]. Investors should read this seasonal swing with care. Negative cash flow in H1 is built into the contract model, provided Q4 collections clear the receivable bulge [1, 4, 14].

web_blocks.title: Cleanroom & Test-Range Leverage: Why Fixed Assets Turn Slowly But Defend Margins
paragraphs: Astra's gross fixed assets plus CWIP stood at ₹276 Cr in Mar 2026 (rising to ₹310 Cr by Sep 2026) against ₹1,163 Cr of revenue—a respectable ~4.2x fixed-asset turn [1]. The real capital trap is not machinery, but working capital: 'Other Assets' (predominantly inventories and trade receivables) reached ₹1,662 Cr in Mar 2026 and ₹1,840 Cr by Sep 2026, representing 83% of the ₹2,206 Cr balance sheet [1].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand how money actually moves through Astra Microwave, forget everything you know about consumer brands or software companies. Astra has no retail storefronts, no distributors, and no advertising budget. Its entire sales engine is an engineering-led qualification funnel inside India's defence and space laboratories—DRDO's LRDE and DLRL, Bharat Electronics, Hindustan Aeronautics, ISRO, and the India Meteorological Department.

Once Astra's RF engineers spend three to five years co-developing a radar array or electronic warfare receiver alongside a DRDO lab, that part number gets frozen into the platform's bill of materials. A rival cannot simply walk in with a 5 percent lower quote and steal the order, because requalifying a new RF subsystem across thermal shock, vibration, and EMI/EMC chambers takes years and risks delaying an entire fighter or missile programme. That is why Astra's switching costs are genuinely structural.

Now walk with me onto the supply chain side, because that is where the friction lives. Astra's factories in Hyderabad—five units across Bollaram and Maheshwaram—and its system-integration hub at the Bengaluru Aerospace Park are world-class, complete with Class 10,000 cleanrooms and a 17-metre Near Field Antenna Test Range. Yet the raw silicon and gallium nitride MMIC dies at the heart of those modules are still imported from specialised foundries abroad. Because Indian defence contracts penalise late deliveries, Astra has to buy and hold critical components months in advance. That is why inventory sat at 394 days in FY26.

Let us trace every 100 rupees of FY26 revenue through the unit economics waterfall so you can see the exact cost structure. Out of 1,163 crore rupees in consolidated sales, materials and inventory consumed 50.5 rupees per 100, specialised engineering payroll took 13.3 rupees, and other operating expenses took 7.5 rupees. That left an impressive 28.7 rupees of operating profit—a massive step up from the 12 rupees per 100 Astra earned during its export-heavy FY21 and FY22 years. After 3.8 rupees for depreciation, 4.8 rupees for interest, 2.2 rupees of other income, and 5.8 rupees for taxes, 16.6 rupees dropped to the bottom line as net profit.

Why did interest eat nearly 5 rupees out of every 100? Look at the balance sheet: out of 1,988 crore rupees of total assets in March 2026, only 276 crore rupees sat in fixed plants and equipment, while 1,662 crore rupees sat in current assets—mostly inventory and government receivables. With 216 debtor days and 42 percent of annual revenue bunching into the March quarter, Astra has to finance a 537-day cash conversion cycle. When collections finally arrive, as they did in FY26 when operating cash flow hit 387 crore rupees, the cash gusher is real—but you and I must never confuse a single year's collection surge with an asset-light business.

Let us trace why that seasonal accordion happens every single year inside India's defence supply chain. Public-sector integrators like HAL and BEL, along with DRDO labs, operate under government fiscal budgets that expire on March 31. Inspection teams, DGAQA quality-assurance sign-offs, and milestone payment releases cluster heavily into the final ninety days of the fiscal year. Meanwhile, Astra cannot wait until January to order gallium nitride chips from overseas foundries; if it did, it would miss delivery windows and trigger liquidated-damages penalties.

So Astra's treasury runs a predictable two-step dance. From April through December, it draws down short-term cash credit lines to buy imported MMICs and build sub-assemblies into work-in-progress—which is why borrowings climbed back to 487 crore rupees by September 2026. Then, between January and March, finished radar arrays clear acceptance testing, Q4 revenue explodes—hitting 488 crore rupees in March 2026 alone—and customer cheques arrive to pay down the credit lines. As long as those cheques clear on time, the unit economics of 28.7 rupees of EBITDA per 100 rupees of sales remain exceptionally healthy. The moment a government budget freezes or an inspection slips past March 31, however, that entire 537-day working-capital cycle sits on Astra's balance sheet.

Now follow a ₹100 customer invoice from Astra Microwave's cleanrooms in Hyderabad and Bengaluru to the bank account. Unlike consumer brands that sell through distributors and collect cash upfront, Astra Microwave operates in a strict B2G and Tier-1 defense OEM ecosystem—selling directly to DRDO, BEL, HAL, ISRO, and the Ministry of Defence. Every program requires years of environmental stress screening, NABL-accredited EMI/EMC testing, and 17-meter Near-Field Antenna Test Range (NFTR) calibration before a single production batch is accepted.

Look at the FY26 audited ₹100 waterfall: out of every ₹100 of consolidated revenue (₹1,163 crore), raw materials and imported MMIC/semiconductor components consume roughly ₹54, employee costs take ₹12, and other operating expenses take ₹5, leaving ₹29 in operating profit (EBITDA). After ₹4 of depreciation, ₹3 of interest, and ₹6 of taxes (net of other income), roughly ₹17 drops to net profit (PAT of ₹193 crore). In FY26, a massive Q4 collection surge pushed operating cash flow to ₹33 per ₹100 of sales (₹387 crore), and after ₹8 of capex, free cash flow hit ₹25 per ₹100. Yet as we will see in Chapter 6, FY26 was the exception, not the 12-year rule.

Every step in Astra Microwave's supply chain underscores why working capital is structurally heavy. Specialized Gallium Nitride (GaN) and Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) monolithic microwave integrated circuits (MMICs), high-frequency laminates, and precision connectors must be procured from global semiconductor foundries months ahead of assembly. Once subsystems are built in Hyderabad or Bengaluru, they undergo thermal cycling, vibration testing, and chamber calibration before final customer acceptance—stretching inventory days to 394 days before a receivable is even raised.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Astra's factories are not capital-intensive; its balance sheet is working-capital-intensive. The cleanrooms and test ranges turn over more than four times a year, but the 537-day cash conversion cycle means every growth spurt demands upfront cash for imported silicon and patient waiting for government milestone cheques.
